Author: namibj
Content:
If not yet, then it's _definitely_ something we'd want to cover; if you're particularly interested in this, I'd suggest you make a plan for a circuit that is small and that could measure this with the only external connections being a clock signal (AC-coupled, for example through some level-shifter-esque CMOS inverter that uses the gate oxide as the AC-coupling capacitance) of around a couple hundred kHz to a couple MHz, perhaps if needed a couple 10's of MHz, and a few kelvin-connected power+sense wire (pairs) off of an analog MUX towards that DUT.
Like, there would be high-mux-resistance sense wires with lower leakage and probably lower-mux-resistance drive wires with higher leakage available, about half/half split I'd guess so far, that would be muxed to the DUT to normally provide multi-terminal DC bias operating point e-tests of small relevant cells using SPICE runs to automatically match/line-up bias drive conditions that are interesting/worthwhile to cover for the stack of dies.

Edit: you'd perhaps measure DC current draw proportional to clock frequency of something that's electrically approximately a small inverter with the capacitance-test-subject as it's load capacitance, and a second such inverter laid out according to matched pair analog design rules that could be measured with no load capacitance for reference.
I think personally I'd want to make that inverter be actually separate push/pull transistors fed from something that cooks up a dead time for the transition such that there's no shoot-through of the "technically a half-bridge" that's wiggling the DUT load capacitance.
Like, a couple delay buffers delaying the edge and then a NAND between delayed and original clock to the PMOS and a NOR between delayed and original clock to the NMOS.

Author: namibj
Content:
I would quite like to see a thing based on them, btw.
I'm not feeling like they're gonna be _tooo_ suited to getting tested using "muxed e-test", so please feel free to do something that could test/validate them for us and allows to see how well simulation matches reality.

I'm still looking forward to eventually designing and PoC-ing an energy-harvesting (from a capacitive divider/isolator that has a small capacitor a fraction of the effective output capacitance of the 100~300 V transistor the wafer.space die would be controlling the gate of);
I _think_ an LDNMOS with source to local GND, drain to LV-side of that dividing-capacitor;
plus an LDPMOS with source to a local storage/decoupling/buffer capacitor (unregulated) and drain also to the LV-side of that dividing-capacitor (and thus also the LDNMOS drain), though given the voltage rating of it, the schottkey diode _might_ be better, not sure....
could thus select right ahead of a turn-off event of the high voltage power transistor whether to feed the charge pulse into the storage cap or whether to skip it this time, 
where accepting the charge is to turn the LDNMOS off and.... I guess _eventually_ the LDPMOS on (ideally timed to not wastefully charge the drain node from the storage cap and burn a good chunk of that energy flow... bonus for schottkey auto-timing!).
And skipping the charge would be to keep the LDNMOS on and the LDPMOS off so that that charge is shunted/bypassed through GND.
Ahead of turn-on, LDPMOS should be off and LDNMOS (back) on to grab that charge.... Hmmm, I _guess_ using a schottkey as well for that part might make the entire setup something that could _decently_ bootstrap off of it until the local supply capacitor has enough to trip a POR mechanism....

...Yep, <https://wiki.restarters.net/Power_supplies#Capacitive_dropper_power_supplies> except that this doesn't have the cycle-skipping NMOS across D2.

Yes it'd also need a regulator from this storage capacitor down to 5V. In theory it could even select between one of several local storage capacitors kept close to the desired supply voltage to not drop as much power across the LDO, but more than two (digital core and something for doing 0 to 5 V gate swings (peak) at the ASIC's output aka into the power transistor) don't sound too useful 😄
